n: In this lecture we are introduced to forensic toxicology. Toxicology comes from the Greek words toxikon, meaning poison, and logos, meaning study. It is the science of poisonous substances and poisoning, divided into general and special. General toxicology studies the regularities of the action of poisons. Special toxicology studies the properties of individual poisons and methods of treatment. Now this science is divided into forensic, industrial, food and military toxicology.

We begin with the concept of poison. There is no absolute poison: a substance, having entered the organism, may have a poisonous property only under certain conditions. A poison causes poisoning by its chemical or physico-chemical properties and must act even when it enters in a small amount. Thus in forensic medicine a poison is a substance that, even in a small amount, impairs health or leads to death.

The classification of poisonous substances is made by the nature of action on organs and tissues. There are two large groups: poisons of local and of general action. Those of local action are divided into two kinds. Corrosives include acids, alkalis, formalin and phenol. Destructives include salts of heavy metals, organochlorine pesticides, phosphorus, corrosive sublimate and arsenic. Poisons of general action are also of two kinds. The first are those acting on the blood: carbon monoxide, potassium chlorate, aniline, nitrobenzene and nitrites. The second are poisons acting on the nervous system.

t: Poisons acting on the nervous system
n: Poisons acting on the central and peripheral nervous system are divided into four subgroups. The first group paralyse the central nervous system, that is, the CNS. The second group depress CNS activity. The third group excite the CNS and cause convulsions. The fourth group are poisons acting mainly on the peripheral nervous system. Remember, this division is made by the main target of the poison.

In examination, together with the physico-chemical properties of the poison, the conditions of its action on the organism are also taken into account. These conditions fall into four groups. The first are conditions depending on the poison: dose, solubility, concentration. The second depends on the individual state of the organism: age, health, weight, sex. The third depends on the route of entry: intravenous, airways, stomach. The fourth depends on the external environment: temperature and humidity.

t: Conditions depending on the poison: lethal dose
n: Of the conditions depending on the poison, the most important is the lethal dose. The lethal dose is the minimum amount of poison causing the death of a person. Examples: atropine 0.1 g; arsenic and morphine 0.2 g; hydrocyanic acid 0.06 g; potassium cyanide 0.15-0.25 g. For acids the dose is given in millilitres: concentrated sulphuric acid 5 ml, nitric acid 5-10 ml, hydrochloric acid 10-15 ml. These figures show the difference between substances.

Now about solubility, physical state and concentration. A substance insoluble in the juices of the body does not poison: insoluble calomel is harmless, while soluble corrosive sublimate is a strong poison. Gaseous substances are absorbed into the blood directly in large amounts, whereas some poisons act faster by mouth. Concentration is also important: dilute hydrochloric acid is a medicine, and concentrated is a strong poison. Moreover, 48-96% acetic acid may lead to death.

t: Conditions of intake and shelf life
n: The conditions of intake also change the action of a poison. An alkaline medium speeds the absorption of arsenic, an acid medium, for example sour wine, that of cyanide, and milk and fatty food that of organophosphorus compounds. Strong tea and coffee weaken the action of alkaloids, that is, morphine, strychnine and atropine. An example of shelf life: the potassium cyanide given to Rasputin in December 1916, stored for a long time without oxygen, combined with CO2, turned into potash and was neutralised.

t: Conditions depending on the organism: age and health
n: Now the conditions depending on the organism, first of all age and health. Infants and small children are very sensitive to opium and alcohol, and relatively little to strychnine. It is known from the literature that a three-year-old child died from a small glass of vodka. In chronically ill and emaciated persons a poison acts quickly and strongly. In kidney disease even a therapeutic dose causes cumulation and severe poisoning. For paediatricians this is very important.

Weight, sex and habituation. The lethal dose is directly related to the victim's weight, since a poison is distributed to organs and tissues. During menstruation and pregnancy the female organism is considerably more sensitive to poisons. A person habituated to narcotics, that is, alcohol, morphine and cocaine, receives a large dose. This dose can cause the death of small children.

Repeated intake of a poison creates a pathological stable bond. To achieve the effect the dose is raised: morphine addicts bring it from 0.01-0.02 g to 0.3-0.5 g. If intake stops, the abstinence syndrome develops: the activity of the entire nervous system and internal organs is disturbed, and a drug addict is capable of even a grave crime to obtain the drug. Idiosyncrasy is increased sensitivity. Antibiotics, quinine, iodine and novocaine can cause it even in therapeutic doses.

t: Dependence on route of entry and external environment
n: Dependence on the route of entry and on the external environment. When injected into a blood vessel, a poison acts fastest. Some poisons act only by a definite route: chloroform is well absorbed on inhalation and poorly in the stomach. Curare, injected under the skin, paralyses rapidly, but through the stomach is ineffective. In the external environment, in a bath house, bathroom and boiler room, the temperature and humidity create favourable conditions for carbon monoxide poisoning. Low temperature creates a tendency to alcohol poisoning.

Poisoning is divided into three periods. Acute poisoning occurs in a toxic or lethal dose and lasts from minutes to a day; with hydrocyanic acid and carbon monoxide death occurs rapidly. Subacute poisoning begins slowly after a single intake and extends to 1-2 weeks, for example with mercuric chloride; the internal organs are damaged first. In chronic poisoning a small amount enters repeatedly, for example tetraethyl lead and lead; death may occur even after weeks or months.

Toxicodynamics studies the mechanism of action of a poison. Some poisons, by irritating the sensory nerve fibres at the site of entry, cause reflex shock; this is characteristic of corrosive poisons. Most poisons, however, are resorptive: they act after absorption into the blood and often act selectively. Selective action is manifested in three directions: on haemoglobin, that is, those acting on the blood; on the brain and spinal cord, that is, cerebrospinal; and on the heart, that is, intracardiac.

We distinguish three stages of the action of a poison. In primary action the poison acts on the organ directly. In secondary action, as a result of the primary injury, the function of other organs is disturbed. Example: a haemolytic poison primarily causes haemolysis of the blood, while impairment of kidney function is secondary. Metatoxic action is the late complications: corrosive sublimate causes prolonged damage to the kidneys and renal failure even after the poison has been eliminated.

t: Points of application of a poison
n: The points of application of a poison are known. Arsenic blocks the sulphydryl group of tissue enzymes. Hydrocyanic acid interacts with cytochrome oxidase. Organophosphorus substances act on cholinesterase and disturb the transmission of nerve excitation. There are also synaptic poisons: tetrodotoxin acts on axons, botulinum toxin disturbs the release of acetylcholine, curare the contact of acetylcholine, and sarin the breakdown of acetylcholine.

Having entered the organism, a poison is neutralised, oxidised, reduced and combined with other substances. Poisons interact: synergists strengthen the action, for example sleeping drugs and alcohol; antagonists weaken it, for example acid and alkali. The routes of elimination vary. Through the kidneys the water-soluble are eliminated, through the liver arsenic, through the lungs gaseous substances. Through the stomach morphine and strychnine are eliminated, and through the intestine mercury. Through saliva and sweat phenol is eliminated, and through milk morphine and alcohol.

The examination of poisoning has its own difficulties. At autopsy the clinical signs of poisoning are often unknown. Many poisons leave no specific changes in the human organism. In many poisonings similar autopsy signs make diagnosis difficult. If poisoning is suspected or established, it is obligatory to notify the investigating authorities.

t: Questions of examination and sources of proof
n: The questions resolved by the examination: whether poisoning occurred, with which poison, by which route it entered, that is, through the stomach, airways or under the skin, and in what dose. There are three sources of proof. The first is the period before death and before the opening of the corpse, that is, the circumstances and the clinical picture. The second is the external and internal examination of the corpse. The third is laboratory examinations, that is, forensic chemical and other methods.

t: First source: circumstances and clinical picture
n: The first source is the circumstances and the clinical picture. The circumstances show the possibility of poisoning: porters drank from a container disguised as “spirit” and died in a short time; dichloroethane was found in the corpse. A characteristic clinical sign, as in alcohol poisoning, makes it possible to make a provisional diagnosis before the autopsy. Vomiting before death is frequent in poisoning. But it also occurs in raised intracranial pressure, tumour and intracerebral haemorrhage.

t: Case analysis: an intoxicated man and an epidural haematoma
n: Case analysis: an intoxicated man and an epidural haematoma. A young man was brought from the street to hospital unconscious. He smelled of alcohol, and there were traces of vomit on his clothing. The physician, considering it alcohol poisoning, washed out the stomach; a few hours later the patient died. At autopsy a fracture of the cranial vault and an epidural haematoma were found. That is, the head injury was not detected in time. Conclusion: it is dangerous to make a diagnosis relying on a single sign, for example the smell of alcohol.

t: Case analysis: a three-year-old girl and pyramidon
n: Another case: a three-year-old girl and pyramidon. The girl was brought unconscious, with convulsions and shallow, wheezing breathing; the father said she “slipped and fell”. On spinal puncture, fluid mixed with thick blood was obtained. On opening the skull no blood was found, and the girl died. On forensic chemical examination, pyramidon was found in the internal organs: before the fall the girl had taken 10 tablets. This example shows that poisoning in children may look like a fall.

In inspection of the scene, a suicide note and residues of poison in various containers may be found. Even empty containers are taken for examination, since a rinsing may reveal the poison in the laboratory. Vomit, faeces and gastric washings are collected in a special container, wrapped and sent to the laboratory.

t: Poison in vomit and food: difficulties
n: There are difficulties connected with poison in vomit and food. Sometimes poison is found in the vomit but not in the internal organs, because it has been destroyed or eliminated. Suspicious substances are taken by the investigator, wrapped, sealed and sent for forensic chemical examination. Complaints that there is poison in food or drink are often related to mentally ill persons or family conflicts.

t: Second source: external examination of the corpse
n: The second source is external examination of the corpse. If the lividity is bright red, it is carbon monoxide; if brown, methaemoglobin-formers, that is, potassium chlorate, aniline, nitrites. In poisoning with the death cap, rigor mortis may not be observed at all; in strychnine it is strongly developed. With a corrosive poison there are patches around the mouth, in atropine the pupil is dilated, and in a haemolytic poison the skin and sclerae turn yellowish.

t: Order of internal examination of the corpse
n: The order of internal examination of the corpse. When poisoning is suspected, water and antiseptics are not used at autopsy, because the poison could be washed away. Attention is paid to the smell of the internal organs: alcohol, acetic acid, ammonia solution, cyanide compounds. The order is as follows. First the heart is opened and blood taken. Then the stomach and intestines are separated, with the entrance and exit tied. The stomach and intestine are opened separately.

Tests and taking of material. First, preliminary chemical tests are carried out: litmus paper, the Hoppe-Seyler test, examination of the blood with a spectroscope. If the poison is unknown, the stomach, 1 m of intestine, 1/3 of the liver with the gallbladder, one kidney and urine are taken into a glass container. Also taken are 1/3 of the brain, heart blood, spleen and 1/4 of the lung. The material taken must not be preserved with formalin or spirit. With spirit and nitrites, urgent delivery is necessary.

The third source is forensic chemical examination. In the referral the expert states the preliminary information, the result of the autopsy, the pathological diagnosis and the reason for suspecting poisoning. The chemist isolates substances from the biological material, determines the quality and quantity, and evaluates them. The difficulty is that it is hard to isolate a small amount of poison from material of large mass: there are impurities.

Exhumation and preservation of poison. In exhumation, samples are taken of clothing, coffin lining, ornaments, paints and soil, 6 samples in all, since poison may have passed from the ground. Alcohol and potassium cyanide break down quickly. Arsenic, salts of heavy metals and strychnine are well preserved. With polarography, lead was proved in the bones of a corpse buried several years earlier.

t: A chemical finding is not always proof
n: A chemical finding is not always proof. Finding a poison does not always prove poisoning: it may enter the corpse after death from the coffin lining, clothing or a dirty vessel. Some poisons enter with a medicine or food, for example arsenic, bismuth, table vinegar. Alcohol, potassium chlorate and cocaine may be eliminated before death. Chloroform, atropine and acetic acid may break down after death.

There are also other laboratory methods. The histological method is important for haemolytic poisons, salts of heavy metals in the kidney, and corrosive poisons in the gastrointestinal tract. The pharmacological method is carried out on animals: in the frog one millionth of a gram of strychnine is detected, and in the cat one ten-thousandth of atropine. The botanical method identifies the poisonous plant, and the biochemical method cholinesterase activity, that is, an organophosphorus poison. Physical methods include spectrography, chromatography and radiography.

We turn to corrosive poisons of local action. Corrosive substances cause a local chemical burn and tissue necrosis; once absorbed into the blood they also have a general action. Acids, with free hydrogen ions, dehydrate tissue and coagulate protein. As a result dry, that is, coagulative, necrosis forms. Necrotic tissue with altered blood takes on a brownish-reddish and black colour, with inflammation at the edge.

t: Acid poisoning: clinical picture and death
n: The clinical picture and death in acid poisoning. Lethal dose: sulphuric acid 5 ml, nitric 5-10 ml, hydrochloric 10-15 ml, acetic 15-20 ml. There is severe pain in the oesophagus and stomach, the vomit is bloody, and pieces of necrotic mucous membrane are found in the vomit. In the first hour death results from shock, asphyxia or internal bleeding; often on day 1-2 from severe intoxication. Then pneumonia, renal failure, mediastinitis and peritonitis develop.

t: Sulphuric acid and changes in the corpse
n: Sulphuric acid and changes in the corpse. Around the mouth of the corpse there are yellowish-grey or brown parchment-like patches; these are traces of a chemical burn. On internal examination the oesophageal mucosa is hardened and dirty grey. In the stomach there is an acid brown fluid with pieces of detached mucosa, and sometimes perforation of the wall is observed. In death after 2-4 days, toxic necronephrosis is found in the kidney, fatty dystrophy in the liver, pneumonia and peritonitis.

Hydrochloric, nitric and acetic acids. In hydrochloric acid the changes are characteristic of the other corrosive acids, but less marked than with sulphuric acid. In nitric acid, nitrogen combines with tissue protein, that is, by the xanthoproteic reaction, and stains the tissue yellow-green. In acetic acid bronchopneumonia develops through the airways. In general action, haemolysis of erythrocytes and haemoglobinuria are observed, then renal failure and uraemia.

Alkalis, with hydroxyl ions, dissolve protein, forming alkaline albuminate. This is wet, that is, colliquative, necrosis: the tissue is soft, swollen and slippery. The lethal dose of caustic soda and potash is 10-15 ml; death often occurs in the first day. Phenol, that is, carbolic acid, acts with its whole molecule and is also absorbed through the skin. It quickly relieves pain, but the general signs increase. The lethal dose of phenol is ~10 ml.

Of the poisons of general action, carbon monoxide, that is, carbon oxide. It is colourless and odourless; it forms in incomplete combustion of organic substances, for example in faulty gas appliances, garages, fires and mines. Mechanism: carbon monoxide enters in breathing, combines with haemoglobin and forms carboxyhaemoglobin, so oxygen transport is impaired. It also combines with myoglobin, making the muscles dark red. Death results from respiratory paralysis when 70-80% of the haemoglobin has been converted to carboxyhaemoglobin. When the content in the air is above 1%, a fulminant form is observed.

t: Carbon monoxide: signs on the corpse and diagnosis
n: In death from carbon monoxide the lividity is dark red, the blood fluid and bright red; the internal organs and muscles are of the same colour. For diagnosis, carboxyhaemoglobin is determined in the blood. At 60-70% there are unconsciousness and respiratory depression; at 80% or more death occurs at once. Chemical examination may be negative: in rapid death from a high concentration, or if the victim was taken into fresh air. For the sample, 10 ml of blood is taken from large deep vessels.
